strengths: Well-motivated clinical problem: standard deep learning CT reconstruction architectures overfit to a specific sampling rate and grid discretization, whereas clinical settings regularly change view subsampling protocols and target resolutions.

Principled adaptation of Neural Operators (NO) to CT physics: the authors effectively integrate tomographic symmetries into DISCO by developing a rotation-equivariant sinogram operator via flipped circular padding and combining spatial with detector-frequency processing motivated by the Fourier slice theorem.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation across multiple medical datasets (AAPM Low-Dose CT, C4KC-KiTS Kidney CT, and LIDC-IDRI Lung CT) and multiple sparse-view regimes (9, 18, 36, 72 views), achieving substantial quantitative gains (typically 2-4 dB PSNR improvement over unrolled CNN baselines).
Strong demonstration of resolution-agnostic properties, including zero-shot super-resolution on both image grids (256 to 512) and sinogram spaces without retraining.

Thorough ablation and complexity analysis: the paper cleanly separates the contributions of image-space NO, sinogram-space NO (spatial vs. frequency branches), rotation equivariance, and FLOP/runtime trade-offs at training vs. inference.
weaknesses: While the adaptation to CT geometry (flipped circular padding and 1D FFT along the detector axis) is neat, the underlying architectural backbone (DISCO / UDNO) is largely adapted from recent prior work in neural operators and compressed sensing MRI (e.g., Jatyani et al., 2025; Liu-Schiaffini et al., 2024).

In the unrolled scheme (Eq. 4), the physical data consistency step involves the forward Radon operator A and its adjoint A*. The paper could more clearly specify how continuous function space evaluation is reconciled with the discrete implementation of A and A* during multi-resolution / super-resolution inference.
Qualitative visualization figures (e.g., Fig. 4, 5, and 7) are quite small, with small inset difference/zoom areas that make fine structural artifact comparison difficult to assess visually.

strengths: Principled and novel formulation: Applying Neural Operators—specifically Discrete-Continuous (DISCO) convolutions—to sparse-view CT reconstruction directly targets a significant practical bottleneck in clinical CT: handling variable scan geometries, view subsampling rates, and spatial resolutions with a single unified model.

Geometry- and physics-informed architectural design: The proposed framework introduces several CT-tailored designs, notably the dual-domain processing ($NO_s$ and $NO_i$), the Fourier-slice-motivated dual spatial/frequency sinogram branches, and the rotation-equivariant sinogram convolution via flipped circular padding respecting the $\pi$-periodicity Radon symmetry.

Comprehensive empirical validation: CTO is evaluated across three diverse CT datasets (AAPM low-dose abdominal CT, KiTS19 kidney CT, and LIDC-IDRI lung CT). It achieves substantial quantitative improvements (>3 dB PSNR over CNN baselines and competitive/superior results over diffusion baselines) while running >500x faster than diffusion models at inference.

Thorough ablation studies and complexity analyses: The paper and supplement provide detailed ablations isolating the impact of the sinogram vs. image operators, frequency vs. spatial sinogram branches, rotational equivariance padding, DISCO kernel hyperparameter sensitivities, and runtime/FLOP complexity comparisons.
weaknesses: Clarification on scan geometries (parallel-beam vs. fan-beam): The mathematical derivation of the rotation equivariance and flipped circular padding ($p(\theta+\pi, r) = p(\theta, -r)$) in Section 4.1 and Supplementary Section A assumes parallel-beam CT geometry. However, Section B.1 notes that the AAPM dataset uses fan-beam geometry sampled over $[0, 2\pi)$. The paper should clarify how the boundary conditions and rotational symmetries are handled or adapted when transitioning from parallel-beam to fan-beam geometries.

Zero-shot image super-resolution evaluation protocol: In Section 5.3, testing zero-shot super-resolution involves bilinearly upsampling the intermediate representation from $256 \times 256$ to $512 \times 512$ before processing with $NO_i$. While DISCO operates with continuous kernels, relying on bilinear interpolation for inter-grid transfer is a discrete heuristic; evaluating direct continuous coordinate querying or discussing the impact of interpolation artifacts would strengthen the claims.

Baseline multi-rate conditioning: In Table 1, standard CNN and transformer baselines are trained across multiple view counts jointly, where they appear to suffer from lack of rate awareness. It would be valuable to discuss or compare against baselines augmented with simple rate-conditioning mechanisms (e.g., AdaLN or view-count embeddings) to confirm that the gains stem specifically from operator learning rather than mere capacity to handle multi-rate inputs.

strengths: Principled and practical formulation: The paper effectively addresses the rigid discretization and sampling-rate dependency of existing sparse-view CT reconstruction models by formulating CT reconstruction in continuous function space via neural operators.

Domain- and physics-informed architectural design: The adaptation of Discrete-Continuous (DISCO) convolutions to CT—incorporating a dual-domain framework, a dual-branch sinogram operator leveraging the Fourier slice theorem along the detector axis, and flipped circular padding to capture parallel-beam symmetries—is well-motivated by tomographic physics.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed CTO is evaluated across multiple standard CT datasets (AAPM Low-Dose, KiTS19, and LIDC-IDRI) against a wide variety of baselines, including classical solvers, unrolled CNNs, transformer models, and diffusion models.

Strong performance and efficiency: CTO consistently outperforms CNN baselines and diffusion methods (achieving >3 dB PSNR gains over unrolled CNNs and DPS) while maintaining inference speeds (~0.065s) that are orders of magnitude faster than diffusion sampling.

Thorough ablations: The supplementary and main text contain extensive analysis regarding individual component contributions (NOs vs. NOi, spatial vs. frequency branches, circular padding equivariance), hyperparameter importance, and inference FLOPs/parameters.
weaknesses: Discrepancy in acquisition geometry and symmetry formulation: The mathematical justification for rotational equivariance and the pi-periodicity flip identity (Eqs. 8, 10, 15) strictly holds for parallel-beam CT. However, the AAPM dataset uses fan-beam geometry over [0, 2pi), where ray symmetries involve fan-angle shifts rather than a simple flip across r. The authors should clarify how this symmetry applies to or was adapted for fan-beam geometry.

Limited novelty of core operator: The underlying discrete-continuous convolution (DISCO) and U-shaped operator architectures are largely adopted from prior work (e.g., Liu-Schiaffini et al., 2024; Jatyani et al., 2025). The primary novelty lies in tailoring these blocks to the CT pipeline and sinogram symmetries.

Evaluation protocol for zero-shot super-resolution: In Section 5.3, the transition from 256x256 to 512x512 relies on bilinear upsampling before feeding features into the image-space operator. A true continuous function-space evaluation would query continuous coordinates directly rather than relying on standard interpolation heuristics.

Lack of clinical/task-based metrics: While RMSE in Hounsfield Units (HU), PSNR, and SSIM are thoroughly reported, the paper does not evaluate downstream clinical tasks (e.g., lesion detectability, organ segmentation, or contrast-detail preservation), which are important for validating claims of clinical readiness in medical imaging.

strengths: Principled adaptation of Neural Operators to CT reconstruction: The paper successfully leverages continuous function space learning via Discrete-Continuous convolutions (DISCO) to tackle the long-standing limitation of DL-based CT reconstruction being bound to fixed acquisition grids.

Well-grounded physical and geometric inductive biases: Designing the sinogram operator in its native polar coordinates (theta, r) with flipped circular padding effectively respects the rotational equivariance and pi-periodicity-with-flip symmetry of parallel-beam CT. Incorporating the Fourier-slice-inspired 1D detector-axis frequency branch further bolsters reconstruction fidelity.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: CTO shows substantial quantitative gains (3-4 dB PSNR improvement) over classical iterative, CNN-based unrolled, transformer, and diffusion baselines across multiple undersampling rates (9, 18, 36, 72 views) on both KiTS and AAPM datasets, while running orders of magnitude faster than diffusion-based methods.

Zero-shot generalization capability: The paper convincingly demonstrates zero-shot super-resolution both in the image space (256x256 to 512x512) and the sinogram view space (72 to 144 views) without retraining or fine-tuning, substantiating the discretization-agnostic claim of neural operators.
weaknesses: Confounded comparison with the unrolled CNN baseline: Section B.2 specifies that the Unrolled CNN baseline operates entirely in the image space without any sinogram-domain module, whereas CTO includes the dual-branch sinogram operator NOs. This makes it difficult to disentangle whether the ~3-4 dB gain comes from switching from standard convolutions to DISCO or simply from adding a dual-domain sinogram enhancement stage.

Theoretical mismatch in fan-beam geometry: The symmetry group actions and pi-periodicity-with-flip relations (Eqs. 7–15) strictly hold for parallel-beam CT. However, the AAPM dataset is acquired in fan-beam geometry (Sec. B.1). The manuscript does not clearly clarify how fan-beam geometry was handled regarding circular padding and rotational equivariance.

Potential under-training of diffusion baselines: In Section C.1, it is noted that the diffusion model was trained for only 2,000 iterations for a 65M parameter network on 33,000 slices. Typical score-based/diffusion inverse problem setups require tens or hundreds of thousands of steps to converge, raising concerns about whether the diffusion baselines were sufficiently trained.
Minor presentation flaws: A few broken references and typos are present, such as 'Fig.fig:overviewb' on page 4 and 'Mathamatically' on page 6.

strengths: Compelling problem formulation: Standard deep learning reconstruction methods often fail when acquisition resolutions or sampling view counts shift. Formulating accelerated CT reconstruction via neural operators in continuous function space is well-motivated and practically relevant.

Principled integration of CT physical symmetries: The paper effectively incorporates problem-specific domain geometry into the operator design, specifically leveraging the pi-periodicity-with-flip symmetry along the angular and detector axes to ensure rotational equivariance, alongside a 1D Fourier-domain branch motivated by the Fourier slice theorem.

Comprehensive empirical scope across metrics and datasets: The method is validated on both parallel-beam (C4KC-KiTS) and fan-beam (AAPM) geometries, measuring RMSE in Hounsfield Units (HU) as well as PSNR/SSIM across multiple subsampling ratios (18, 36, 72 views) and zero-shot super-resolution scenarios.
weaknesses: Confounded comparison with the unrolled CNN baseline: Section B.2 specifies that the Unrolled CNN baseline consists only of image-space cascades and does not include any learned sinogram-domain processing. Since CTO incorporates an extensive sinogram-space operator (NO_s) with both spatial and frequency branches, it is unclear whether the reported ~3-4 dB improvement arises from the neural operator / DISCO formulation or simply from having a dual-domain (sinogram + image) architecture. An apples-to-apples dual-domain CNN baseline is critical to isolate the contribution of function-space learning.

Substantially undertrained diffusion baselines: In Section B.2 (page 14), the authors state that the diffusion baseline 'was trained for 2,000 iterations' for a 65M-parameter network on a 33,000-slice dataset. At batch size 16, 2,000 iterations corresponds to only ~32,000 image exposures (less than one full epoch over the training data). Diffusion models require orders of magnitude more steps (typically hundreds of thousands of iterations) to converge; benchmarking against an undertrained model weakens the empirical comparison against diffusion-based inverse problem solvers.

Geometric inconsistency in fan-beam CT: The mathematical formulation of the rotational equivariance and the symmetry p(theta + pi, r) = p(theta, -r) strictly holds for parallel-beam CT. However, the AAPM dataset uses a curved fan-beam geometry with source-to-detector distance. In native fan-beam coordinates, the conjugate ray relationship is non-linear and does not correspond to a simple axis flip. The manuscript does not clarify whether fan-to-parallel rebinning was performed or how the boundary conditions behave under native fan-beam geometry.

Missing systematic ablation table: While partial ablations are scattered across the supplement (e.g., Table 5 for circular padding and Fig. 7c for FFT axes), an end-to-end ablation breakdown isolating the individual contributions of NO_s, NO_i, the frequency branch, and continuous discretization kernels is absent from the main text.

strengths: Clear practical motivation: Clinically deployed CT systems frequently vary in angular sampling protocols and reconstruction resolutions; proposing a unified, resolution-agnostic neural operator framework that operates across view settings and resolutions without retraining addresses a major bottleneck of deep learning in this area.

Principled and physics-informed architectural design: The integration of DISCO neural operators into both sinogram and image domains is well grounded. In particular, tailoring the sinogram operator (NOs) with flipped circular boundary conditions to preserve the $\pi$-periodicity-with-flip symmetry of parallel-beam CT, and utilizing a detector-axis Fourier transform inspired by the Fourier Slice Theorem, are theoretically motivated and insightful.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed CTO framework is evaluated against a wide spectrum of baselines—including classical optimization (FBP, SART), dual-domain transformers (DuDoTrans), distillation (GloReDi), and iterative diffusion models (DPS, ALD)—achieving substantial improvements in PSNR/SSIM alongside orders-of-magnitude faster inference compared to diffusion models.

Effective zero-shot super-resolution demonstrations: Experiments demonstrate that CTO successfully generalizes zero-shot across both image resolutions ($256\times 256$ to $512\times 512$) and angular view densities ($72$ to $144$ views), clearly outperforming standard convolutional counterparts.
weaknesses: Potential baseline asymmetry in the dual-domain structure: Section B.2 notes that the Unrolled CNN baseline operates entirely in the image space without learned sinogram-domain processing, whereas CTO employs both a dedicated sinogram operator (NOs) and image-space cascades (NOi). To rigorously isolate the advantage of function-space learning (DISCO) over discrete CNNs, an unrolled dual-domain CNN (having equivalent sinogram and image cascades) should be benchmarked under the same parameter budget.

Ambiguity in handling multi-rate inputs for discrete baselines: The paper notes that a single model is trained jointly across all view rates (9, 18, 36, 72 views). For neural networks defined on discrete grids (e.g., Unrolled CNN, DuDoTrans), it is not clearly specified how inputs of differing view dimensions were processed during training and inference (e.g., whether interpolation, zero-padding, or masking was applied).

Geometry mismatch between parallel-beam symmetries and fan-beam data: Section 4.1 and Supplementary Section A derive rotational equivariance and the $\pi$-periodicity-with-flip identity strictly for parallel-beam geometry. However, Section B.1 states that the AAPM Low-Dose CT dataset utilizes a fan-beam geometry over $[0, 2\pi)$. In fan-beam geometry, image rotations do not simply map to translations in $(\theta, r)$ without rebinning, nor does the exact same flip boundary hold. Clarification on how fan-beam geometry was reconciled with these operators is needed.

Evaluation restricted to 2D slice reconstructions: Clinical CT acquisition is fundamentally 3D (helical or cone-beam). While testing on 2D slices is common in academic benchmarks, the scalability and memory footprint of DISCO operators in full 3D geometries warrant further discussion.
